title: Aniimo Beginner Guide: Catching, Twining and Your First Team
excerpt: A practical first route through catching, Twining, exploration and a four-role starter team.
coverAlt: Aniimo companions exploring a bright fantasy landscape
intro: Aniimo combines creature discovery, action combat and exploration. The fastest start is not collecting everything at once; it is learning what each team slot contributes, then expanding your roster around a clear next objective.
takeaways: Start with one damage option, one support or heal option and one break option
Treat exploration abilities as part of roster value
Use published role, element and skill text before relying on rankings
steps: Open the Aniimo list and identify one damage-focused record you enjoy using.
Add a support, heal or regen option before filling duplicate damage roles.
Choose a break option for tougher encounters, then use the fourth slot to cover a habitat or element need.
Read the published skill and trait text for each candidate before assigning it a job.
Choose one habitat objective for the next session instead of scattering attention across the whole map.
Test the four-slot draft in Team Builder and adjust only one position at a time.

sections.title: Start with jobs, not a perfect roster
sections.body: Every early team benefits from clear jobs. Damage moves an encounter forward; support, healing or regeneration gives you room to recover; break creates a safer opening against resilient targets. You do not need every answer on day one, but naming the missing job gives each future discovery a purpose.

sections.title: Use habitats to set a small, achievable target
sections.body: Pick one or two records that improve the role your team lacks, then check the habitats already listed on their profiles. A short route with a specific target is easier to repeat and evaluate than a vague plan to collect everything in one region.

sections.title: Let the fourth slot remain flexible
sections.body: The final position is where an early roster gains comfort. Use it for an element you do not have, a pathfinding utility, or a second contribution that fits your current activity. Flexibility is more valuable than forcing a theoretical composition before you know the encounter.

sections.title: Read the kit before making an assumption
sections.body: Role labels are a reliable starting point, not a complete rotation guide. Open the profile and scan the published skills, trait and mobility entries before deciding what a creature will do for your party. If a field is not listed, leave it unknown rather than building a plan around a guess.

sections.title: Keep a short review loop
sections.body: After a route or encounter, record one thing that worked and one thing that felt missing. Did a team lack recovery, struggle to create an opening, or simply need a better travel option? Changing a single slot gives you a useful comparison; changing the entire team at once hides what actually improved.

title: Aniimo Forms & Evolution: Regional Forms, Element Changes and Materials
excerpt: Use form differences, published evolution paths and material planning to make better collection decisions.
intro: A form is more than a new portrait. It can change an Aniimo’s stage, elements and base fields, while an evolution path can branch into a different long-term choice. Read those changes before you spend a session chasing a path that does not fit your team.
takeaways: Compare the form you have with the form you want
Read an evolution path from start to finish before making a route
Use materials and habitats as planning clues, not promises of a quick upgrade
steps: Open the Aniimo profile and switch through every available form.
Write down the stage, element or role difference that would actually change your team.
Follow the evolution path to see whether it branches into more than one destination.
Check which habitats and materials connect to the path you want to pursue.
Use the map to combine that route with another collection target when possible.
Return to Team Builder and see what the evolved form would add or replace.

sections.title: Start with the form you already have
sections.body: Open the profile and compare the current form with the form you are considering. Look for a change that matters to your own next activity: a different element, a different stage, or base fields that better support the job you need filled.

sections.title: A branch is a decision point
sections.body: An evolution path may lead forward in a line or split into different destinations. Do not treat every branch as an automatic improvement. Pause at the split and ask which destination gives your roster a clearer option for the activities you actually enjoy.

sections.title: Plan the route before the upgrade
sections.body: Habitats and materials become useful when they help you plan one practical outing. If an evolution target sits beside other Aniimo or collection goals you want, the route does more than chase a single upgrade.

sections.title: Check what changes in the team
sections.body: A new form can add variety, but it can also replace a role your current party relied on. Put the candidate into Team Builder before committing to the route, then see whether the team gained a useful answer or simply doubled up on something it already had.

sections.title: Make one clear comparison
sections.body: If two forms look appealing, compare them against the same question: which one helps the next team slot or route? Keep the comparison narrow enough that the trade-off is visible, then let your own roster decide the final pick.

title: Aniimo Combat Guide: Roles, BREAK, EP and Team Building
excerpt: Build clearer teams by connecting roles, BREAK windows, EP use and elemental coverage.
intro: Elements and roles answer different questions. Elements describe an Aniimo’s affinity, while roles describe its broad contribution to a party. Reading both together is the simplest way to understand where a record may fit.
takeaways: Element and role are separate labels
Role balance is usually more useful than chasing a complete element set
steps: Identify the damage source your team currently relies on.
Add a support, heal or regen record that gives the party recovery or utility.
Add break pressure when you expect tougher targets.
Check whether your first three slots all share the same element or limitation.
Use the remaining slot to solve an element, habitat or exploration gap.
Review the team in the analyzer before changing multiple slots at once.

sections.title: Elements describe affinity
sections.body: The database groups Aniimo by official element labels. Use the element directory when you need to see which records share an affinity or when you want to avoid an overly narrow roster. An element label alone does not tell you whether an Aniimo heals, breaks or deals damage.

sections.title: Roles describe contribution
sections.body: DPS focuses on pressure, Heal and Regen provide recovery, Support improves a party’s options, and Break helps create an opening. Some Aniimo can contribute more than one way, but these labels give you a useful first pass before reading each published skill description.

sections.title: Build coverage around the activity
sections.body: A balanced party is not a checklist of nine elements. Begin with a clear damage source, enough sustain for mistakes and an answer for sturdier targets. Then make the remaining choices based on the habitat, goal and records you want to pursue next.

sections.title: Use dual labels as options, not obligations
sections.body: Some records carry more than one element or role label. That can make a roster more flexible, but it does not mean every possible contribution will be equally important in the same activity. Start from the job you need, then use the additional label as a way to widen future choices rather than a reason to overcomplicate the first team.

sections.title: Evaluate coverage after every swap
sections.body: When you replace one Aniimo, check what left the party as well as what arrived. A new element might improve variety but remove the only sustain option; a second damage record might help a simple route while leaving no answer for a stronger target. Reviewing role and element coverage after each change keeps the decision visible.
